blindSummary:
This state/province carried a state/province-level resolution declaring it free of LGBT ideology from 2020 until its repeal in September 2021, under pressure from a supranational funding body. A town of about 40,000 people here was the first local authority in the country to adopt an anti-LGBT resolution (March 2019, against “LGBT ideology and the early sexualisation of children”), and a deputy council chair explained the act explicitly as opposition to the capital’s LGBT+ equality declaration signed a month earlier. That town became the template copied by roughly 100 authorities nationwide.

The resolution is now formally gone, but as with other state/provinces that copied the template the repeal was coerced rather than converted — the underlying civic mobilisation that produced the country’s first-ever anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto signal. No march violence or ban is documented at the state/province level beyond the general resolution-era hostility.

Local risk sits above the country-wide average: safer than two neighbouring state/provinces — one where the resolution additionally drew a mayoral ban on the march and held out until 2025, and one where a 2019 coordinated mass assault added a violence dimension absent here — but less safe than a neighbouring state/province that pairs its own resolution history with its main city’s clearly positive institutional trajectory.
